terminology_notes: Use Mt. Diablo for the v1.0.0 specification and current architecture. Diablo 400 is the historical project/course name; keep stable source folders, course_slug, module slugs and audio filenames for compatibility.

Say plus-minus 400 volts DC for the bipolar case and differential 800 volts DC for pole-to-pole voltage. Differential voltage alone does not specify voltage to protective earth. Section 8.1.4 also describes floating/high-resistance-return and single-ended solid-return 800 V architectures; do not imply every 800 V output is referenced the same way.

Sections 9 and 10 contain DC and AC interconnect options. Connector part numbers remain preliminary in the final release. Appendix A grounding tradeoffs and Appendix B thermal discussion are non-normative.

slides.title: AI Rack Power Is Moving Faster Than Legacy Architectures

source_refs.source: Microsoft Azure infrastructure blog

slides.subtitle: AI systems are turning power delivery into a rack-level architecture constraint.

bullets.text: Cloud racks that once fit below 20 kW are being joined by AI racks in the hundreds of kilowatts.
Accelerators, networking, memory, and liquid cooling compete with power conversion hardware.
Interconnect density, power delivery, and thermal design now move together.
A disaggregated sidecar lets the IT rack focus on compute while the power rack handles conversion and support.

slides.title: Current, Copper, and I2R Losses

source_refs.source: SemiAnalysis: Inside the 800VDC Revolution - Part 1
Mt. Diablo Disaggregated Power Rack Specification v1.0.0

slides.subtitle: Higher voltage reduces current for the same power, which reduces conductor stress.

bullets.text: For a fixed power target, raising voltage lowers current.
I2R loss rises with the square of current, so high current gets expensive quickly.
Designers spend the gain on smaller conductors, simpler routing, and less heat.
Plus-minus 400 volt distribution keeps current, copper, and serviceability within a practical envelope.

figure_plan.note: Two-path comparison: low voltage/high current/heavy copper versus plus-minus 400 volt distribution/lower current/practical cabling.

figure.alt: Silent animation showing that higher distribution voltage lowers current and I2R loss pressure for the same power target.
figure.caption: At fixed power, higher distribution voltage lowers current and reduces conductor burden.

entries.text: Same power target, different current burden

slides.subtitle: The key move is physical disaggregation: power beside the IT rack, not inside it.

bullets.text: Receives three-phase AC and delivers controlled high-voltage DC toward nearby IT racks.
Preserves space for accelerators, switches, manifolds, and cooling hardware.
Places conversion, distribution, protection, and optional storage in a rack optimized for power work.
A common interface helps suppliers build toward the same handoff point.

slides.title: OCP Tenets and the Rack & Power Home

source_refs.source: OCP Rack & Power Project

slides.subtitle: Mt. Diablo is a shared infrastructure layer, not a one-vendor design pattern.

bullets.text: Defines high-voltage interfaces and mating expectations the community can refine together.
Uses higher-voltage distribution to reduce current and conductor losses.
Targets hundreds of kilowatts and power-rack reuse across IT generations.
Separates longer-lived power infrastructure from faster-moving compute platforms.
Learners should follow future work through the OCP Rack & Power project.

slides.title: Why the Sidecar Matters
items: AI rack density is pushing power into hundreds of kilowatts and toward 1 MW-class infrastructure.
Higher voltage helps control current, copper, heat, and serviceability constraints.
The sidecar model moves conversion, distribution, protection, and optional energy storage out of the IT rack.
OCP standardization gives the ecosystem a common power interface to build around.

slides.title: Check Your Power Architecture Mental Model
slides.subtitle: Submit each question once to continue. Correct answers are not required, and retry is available.

questions.prompt: Why does the Mt. Diablo architecture move major power conversion and support functions into a sidecar rack?

choices.text: To preserve IT rack space and make conversion, protection, distribution, and optional storage serviceable as power infrastructure.
To eliminate the need for three-phase AC input power at the facility level.
To make every compute tray, accelerator, and liquid-cooling manifold identical across vendors.
To remove the need for grounding, protection, and service access controls.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The sidecar pattern disaggregates power so the IT rack can prioritize compute, networking, and cooling while power hardware is serviced in a purpose-built rack.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the sidecar model. The important move is physical disaggregation: power conversion and support functions sit beside the IT rack, not inside it.

questions.prompt: Which challenges does higher-voltage distribution help manage in high-power AI racks?

choices.text: Lower current for a given power target
Reduced conductor heating and I2R losses
More practical copper, routing, and serviceability tradeoffs
Removal of all shock and arc hazards
No need for a shared ecosystem interface

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Higher voltage helps manage current, copper, heat, and practical service constraints, but it does not remove electrical hazards.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the physics slide. Higher voltage helps with current and I2R losses, but protection, grounding, and service practices still matter.

slides.title: What the Power Rack Must Deliver
items: The sidecar is a serviceable AC-to-DC power rack built for high-density deployment.

Dynamic loading and end-to-end efficiency are central Mt. Diablo requirements.

slides.subtitle: Submit each question once to continue. Correct answers are not required, and retry is available.

questions.prompt: What does differential 800 Vdc tell you about a Mt. Diablo output?

choices.text: The voltage between the two output conductors; the grounding architecture still determines voltage to PE.
Every output conductor is always 800 V above PE.
Every two-wire connection must route a common midpoint to the IT rack.
Grounding and input isolation no longer need review.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Differential describes conductor-to-conductor voltage. Midpoint or return grounding determines the earth reference.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the output model and grounding options. Pole-to-pole voltage alone does not specify either pole’s voltage to PE.

questions.prompt: Which items are part of the dynamic loading and efficiency picture in Mt. Diablo?

choices.text: 3 ms transient settling time
50, 90, and 140 percent load steps from 10 percent minimum load
1 amp per microsecond slew rate
Unlimited voltage overshoot during AI load changes
Efficiency measured only inside the IT tray, not end to end

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The spec treats transient behavior and end-to-end efficiency as part of the power-rack requirement set.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Revisit the dynamic loading table. The named requirements include fast settling, defined step loads, and a current slew-rate expectation.

slides.subtitle: The interface layer turns the electrical architecture into serviceable rack hardware.

bullets.text: Accepts up to 16×200 Aac or 24×100 Aac input cords, includes protection fuses, and feeds the power shelves.
Shelves up to 2 OU host 1 OU PSU options. PSU modules are front-accessible, hot-swappable and galvanically isolated.
Up to 400 kW per output module; protection, telemetry, switching, and voltage disconnection before unplugging at either end.
Sections 9–10 cover DC and AC cables. Table 12 includes 50 kW and 100 kW three-wire options plus a 96/100 kW two-wire option; connector part numbers remain preliminary.
Retain PE and two interlock signal contacts. Verify wiring, current rating, mating parts, and disconnect behavior for the selected option.
Single-zone three-conductor distribution for plus, minus, and common, designed for up to 1.1 MW average load power.

entries.text: Follow the power path from facility AC to the IT rack
Facility AC enters from the overhead busway.
The AC PDU accepts input and protects the power shelves.
Hot-swappable PSU modules in the shelves convert power and share current.
The vertical busbar distributes plus, minus, and common.
The DC PDU protects, switches, controls, and reports telemetry.
Output voltage disconnects before a cable is serviced.
Together, the interfaces form a deliberate service path.

slides.subtitle: Separate pole-to-pole voltage from voltage to PE, then verify the selected architecture.

cards.title: ±400 V midpoint reference
cards.body: High-resistance or solid midpoint-to-PE connection. Routing may be 3-wire + PE or 2-wire + PE with no midpoint routed to the IT rack.

cards.title: 800 V return reference
cards.body: Two-wire + PE. Section 8.1.4 describes floating output with high-resistance return reference or single-ended 800 V with return solidly bonded to PE.

cards.title: Detection is required
cards.body: Ground-fault detection is required for both solid and high-resistance midpoint grounding. HRG needs voltage-balance detection; residual-current detection is required per output cable/connection.

cards.title: Protection and compatibility
cards.body: Grounding changes fault current, insulation, bonding, and service practice. Appendix A is non-normative; neither scheme removes pole-to-pole shock risk.

slides.subtitle: The spec leaves room for implementation choices, but names the interfaces operators should expect.

bullets.text: May interface with all Mt. Diablo building blocks inside the sidecar.
Redfish is recommended; proprietary interfaces are allowed when needed.
Ethernet, I2C, PMBus, Modbus, and CAN bus are listed interface options.

slides.title: Safety, EMC, Sustainability, and Implementation Boundaries

source_refs.source: Mt. Diablo Disaggregated Power Rack Specification v1.0.0

slides.subtitle: These requirements are what make the shared architecture buildable and inspectable.

bullets.text: Integrated rack and subcomponents must comply with applicable IEC/UL 62368-1 requirements and national deviations.
AC mains-connected assemblies must withstand 10 kA to 40 kA available short-circuit fault current, depending on application.
Live parts above PS2 limits must not be accessible without interlock, switch, or de-energization method.
Creepage, clearance, overcurrent protection, PE bonding, leakage current, and ground-fault detection all require review.
Battery standards, NFPA 855, CISPR 32/35, emissions, surge, ESD, and environmental regulations are in scope.

slides.title: What to Verify at the Interfaces
items: Verify the cable, mating parts, interlock, and disconnect behavior for the chosen interface.
Identify the grounding and wiring topology before evaluating fault behavior and detection.
Check what telemetry the implementation exposes and how management interfaces integrate.
Review the applicable safety, EMC, and compliance requirements before deployment.

slides.title: Check Your Interface and Safety Boundaries
slides.subtitle: Submit each question once to continue. Correct answers are not required, and retry is available.

questions.prompt: Why does the grounding choice matter for Mt. Diablo implementations?

choices.text: It changes fault behavior, detection and response assumptions, service practice, and compatibility expectations.
It turns the DC output into a low-voltage AC distribution system.
It removes the need to review shock risk between plus and minus poles.
It replaces the need for output protection and disconnect behavior.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. HRG and solid midpoint grounding are design choices with different fault and service implications.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the grounding slide. The choice affects fault behavior and operations; it does not eliminate protection or shock-risk analysis.

questions.prompt: Which requirements or qualifications appear in Mt. Diablo v1.0.0?

choices.text: AC PDU accepts up to 16×200 Aac or 24×100 Aac input cords.
Ground-fault detection is required for solid and high-resistance midpoint grounding.
Residual-current detection is required per output cable/connection to the IT rack.
Connector part numbers in the interconnect tables are preliminary.
Solid midpoint grounding makes ground-fault detection optional.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Check §8.1.1, §8.1.4.2.3, and §§9–10. Final specification status does not make the listed connector part numbers final.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the input-cord limits, mandatory ground-fault and residual-current detection, and the preliminary connector qualification.

slides.subtitle: Coordinate conversion, protection, and storage from the rack to the utility interface.

bullets.text: Bus capacitors can discharge rapidly into a fault. Inductance, converter behavior, and storage location shape the current.
Selectivity aims to isolate the faulted section while keeping healthy loads online.
Solid-state, hybrid, and electromechanical devices trade off clearing speed, losses, and coordination.
Compare a conventional transformer and rectifier with a solid-state transformer. Check isolation and fault response.
Rack storage can buffer fast load swings. Distribution-level storage can support ride-through and grid response.

questions.prompt: Two devices list the same nominal DC system voltage. What should you verify before connecting them?

choices.text: Equipment ratings, continuous and transient voltage limits, and compatibility with the earthing scheme.
Only the displayed nominal voltage, since it fixes the operating band.
choices.feedback_incorrect: Nominal voltage names a system. It does not specify the full voltage range or transient conditions the equipment can handle.

choices.text: Only the peak load, since earthing does not affect device compatibility.
choices.feedback_incorrect: Earthing affects conductor-to-earth voltage during faults and can limit which equipment ratings are compatible.

choices.text: Only the rack's input connector and continuous power rating.
choices.feedback_incorrect: A connector and power rating cannot establish voltage, transient, or earthing compatibility.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Matching nominal voltages is a starting point. The ratings, voltage-time limits, and earthing establish compatibility.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the voltage and topology slide. Compatibility depends on ratings, operating conditions, and earthing.

questions.prompt: What should the team verify across the whole LVDC installation? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Whether protection isolates the faulted section while healthy sections stay online
How the operating sequence handles precharge, rack connection, and fault recovery
How shared-bus noise affects emissions and immunity under representative loads
Only whether each converter has a stand-alone EMC test report
Only whether every rack can energize independently with its local controls

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Selective protection, coordinated operating sequences, and representative EMC tests all address interactions among devices.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the system behavior and verification slides. Stand-alone tests cannot verify how protection, controls, and converters interact.

term_glossary.tooltip: Heat produced when current flows through resistance. Because current is squared, lower current can sharply reduce conductor heating.
Ability of equipment to keep operating through defined voltage or frequency disturbances instead of tripping immediately.
Short-duration stored energy that keeps the supply output alive long enough for another support path to engage after input loss.
Battery backup unit. In Mt. Diablo, an optional energy-storage block that can support 45 to 90 seconds at full load when used.
Capacitor bank unit. In Mt. Diablo, an optional capacitive energy-storage block for short-duration support and transient buffering.
Ratio of active power to apparent power under periodic conditions. Higher values mean the AC input current is being used more effectively.
Total harmonic distortion is a measure of harmonic content in a waveform, used here as an AC input power-quality limit.
Earthing arrangement where neutral and protective-earth functions are carried by separate conductors.
Earthing arrangement where the source is isolated from earth or connected through high impedance, with exposed conductive parts earthed.
Protective conductor path used to bond exposed conductive parts and provide a safer fault-current return path.
Property of a circuit where changing current stores magnetic energy and induces voltage that resists the current change.
Protection coordination that isolates the faulted section while keeping unaffected sections energized where possible.
Hazard from release of energy caused by an electric arc; it can injure people and damage equipment.
Short-circuit current rating. The maximum prospective short-circuit current an assembly is rated to withstand.
Clearance is spacing through air; creepage is spacing along an insulating surface. Both help prevent breakdown or tracking.
Electromagnetic compatibility. Ability of equipment to operate in its electromagnetic environment without causing unacceptable disturbance to other equipment.
DMTF standard for secure, interoperable management of modern IT infrastructure using web-based APIs.
Circuit breaker that uses semiconductor switches to interrupt current rapidly.
Power-electronic transformer that can combine voltage conversion and galvanic isolation in an AC-to-DC system.
Low-voltage direct current. The codes and standards surveyed by the white paper place the upper limit at 1500 V DC.

lms_catalog.short_description: Learn Mt. Diablo v1.0.0 sidecar power for high-density AI racks, with an optional module on facility LVDC.
lms_catalog.overview: Use the OCP Mt. Diablo v1.0.0 specification to understand how a sidecar power rack supports high-density AI racks. Trace the AC-to-DC power path, review rack and management interfaces, and connect grounding, protection, telemetry, EMC, and safety requirements to deployment decisions. An optional module uses the OCP LVDC white paper v1.1.0 to extend the discussion to facility-level DC distribution.
lms_catalog.duration_note: The core path takes approximately 35 minutes. Optional Module 4 adds 15 minutes, for approximately 50 minutes including all modules. Estimates include narration, reading, and knowledge checks; external reference study adds time.

modules.summary: Connect increasing AI rack density to current, copper, and conversion constraints. Explain the sidecar pattern and place Mt. Diablo within OCP rack and power work.
Trace AC input through sidecar building blocks to DC output. Review the physical envelope, power quality, ride-through, energy buffering, dynamic loads, and efficiency requirements.
Review distribution components, grounding choices, management and telemetry, environmental operation, and safety and compliance boundaries. Identify the evidence needed for an implementation review.

Use the OCP LVDC white paper v1.1.0 to connect the Mt. Diablo sidecar to facility and rack architectures. Compare voltage, earthing, protection, and storage choices, and identify what to verify about operating sequences, EMC, and safety.
